claims.text: The formation and persistence of a protective oxide on CrFeCoNiX alloys is governed by the identity and amount of element X.
An optimal Si content promotes formation of a graded mixed Cr2O3/SiO2 scale.
A graded Cr2O3/SiO2 scale minimizes thermal-expansion mismatch and internal stress.
Mn addition leads to unstable, rapidly growing oxide phases that crack or spall.
Excessive Al addition leads to unstable, rapidly growing oxide phases that crack or spall.
The proposed comparison applies to CrFeCoNiX alloys prepared as either single-phase or multiphase metallic solid solutions.
Controlled Si-, Mn-, and Al-containing alloys should be compared with CrFeCoNi containing none of those additions.
The comparison should use exposure above 900 °C for approximately 100–200 hours under controlled oxygen partial pressure and consistent thermal histories.
Oxide-scale chemistry and morphology depend on the alloy chemistry and microstructure.
Scale phase continuity and mechanical integrity mediate whether the oxide remains protective.
Differences in oxygen affinity and oxidation kinetics among Si, Mn, and Al determine the oxidation pathway.
Optimal Si produces controlled, gradual oxidation.
Reduced lattice and thermal-expansion mismatch enhances oxide-scale adhesion.
Mn accelerates oxidation and promotes oxides with large volumetric mismatch.
Excess Al accelerates oxidation and promotes oxides with large volumetric mismatch.
Large oxide-volume mismatch increases internal stress, causing cracking and spallation.
Optimized Si-containing alloys will form thinner, more uniform, and more adherent scales than the CrFeCoNi baseline.
Optimized Si-containing alloys will show less cracking and spallation than Mn-containing or excess-Al-containing alloys.
The hypothesis applies above 900 °C in controlled oxidative or corrosive environments and in composition ranges that minimize phase separation and secondary reactions.
Failure of optimized-Si samples to show statistically significant improvements in coherence, cracking, and adhesion relative to both controls would refute the hypothesis.
